question: The Cash Flow Statement is divided into three sections. Which of the following correctly maps the activity to its section?
before: Under Indian GAAP and Ind AS, interest paid is classified under Cash Flow from Financing Activities (CFF) for non-financial companies — this is a key India-specific nuance. Under US GAAP, interest paid sits under Operations (CFO), so global comparisons require an adjustment. Option A is wrong: buying a factory is a capital expenditure and goes under Cash Flow from Investing (CFI), not Operations. Option B is wrong: issuing equity is a financing activity (raising money from shareholders), so it belongs in CFF, not CFI. Option D is wrong: cash from customers is the lifeblood of the business and belongs in CFO, not Investing. Quick rule of thumb: CFO = day-to-day business, CFI = buying/selling long-term assets, CFF = dealing with lenders and shareholders.
after:
Concept: The Cash Flow Statement classifies all cash movements into three sections: Cash Flow from Operations (day-to-day business activities), Cash Flow from Investing (purchase and sale of long-term assets), and Cash Flow from Financing (raising or repaying capital from lenders and shareholders). Under Indian GAAP and Ind AS, interest paid is classified in Cash Flow from Financing for non-financial companies—a key India-specific rule that differs from US GAAP.

Why this is correct: Interest payments represent cash outflows to external lenders and are treated as a financing activity under Indian standards. This reflects the fact that interest arises from financing decisions (borrowing) rather than operational decisions. Option C correctly identifies both the activity and the classification under Indian reporting frameworks.

Why the others are wrong: Option A—Buying a new factory is a capital expenditure and belongs in Cash Flow from Investing (CFI), not Operations, because it involves acquiring long-term productive assets. Option B—Issuing new equity shares is a financing activity because it represents raising capital directly from shareholders; it belongs in Cash Flow from Financing (CFF), not Investing. Option D—Receiving cash from customers is core operational revenue and belongs in Cash Flow from Operations (CFO), not Investing, because it is the result of selling goods or services in the normal course of business.

Intuition: Understanding the three-way split is critical for equity research because it reveals the quality and sustainability of a company's cash generation. Confusing sections leads to misreading operational strength versus capital intensity. In India, the Ind AS treatment of interest as a financing outflow (rather than operational) can make Indian companies appear to have higher operating cash flow than their US counterparts on the same factual position—an important adjustment when comparing across geographies.
